awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of a Computational Ecosystem for Protein Engineering
awd_abstract_narration:
This I-Corps project focuses on the development of a computational ecosystem for intelligent protein engineering that enables the rapid and efficient design of enzyme variants for applications in biomedicine, biotechnology, and sustainability. The ability to engineer proteins with desired functional properties is essential for addressing challenges in pharmaceutical development, industrial biocatalysis, and environmental remediation. However, traditional experimental approaches are costly and time-intensive, limiting the accessibility of enzyme engineering to a broader range of researchers. The technology provides a scalable, high-throughput solution that integrates molecular modeling with artificial intelligence to streamline protein design. By improving the efficiency of enzyme discovery, this technology enhances the ability to design novel routes for drug synthesis, improve diagnostic tools, and create environmentally friendly catalysts. The adoption of this platform has the potential to significantly reduce industrial waste, lower energy consumption, and accelerate scientific progress in multiple industrial sectors.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of the technology. This solution is based on the development of an integrated computational platform that combines quantum chemistry, molecular simulations, bioinformatics, and machine learning to predict the functional effects of enzyme mutations. The approach leverages high-throughput molecular modeling to generate large datasets of molecular features that augment deep-learning algorithms, improving the accuracy of mutation effect predictions. Unlike traditional experimental screening methods, which rely on costly and time-consuming assays, this computational approach significantly reduces the time and resources required for enzyme optimization. Complementary to existing machine learning models that are trained solely on enzyme sequences, these molecular features inform the structural basis underlying enzyme functions, thereby enhancing the interpretability of the model. The platform's predictive capabilities allow for the rational design of protein variants with enhanced activity, stability, and selectivity, broadening its applicability across pharmaceuticals, industrial enzyme manufacturing, and synthetic biology.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This NSF I-Corps project investigated the translation potential of Mutexa, an AI-Physics-integrated computational ecosystem for protein engineering. Protein engineering optimizes enzymes and peptides to perform useful tasks in biotechnology, medicine, and chemical manufacturing. Mutexa is designed to help scientists identify promising protein or enzyme variants before investing substantial time and resources in laboratory testing.

The project focused on a central commercialization question: can Mutexa address real customer needs in enzyme design, protein property prediction, mutation-effect prediction, and high-throughput virtual screening of functional enzyme candidates? To answer this question, the team conducted 109 customer discovery interviews, including 17 in-person, 90 virtual, and 2 phone interviews. These interviews involved stakeholders from biotechnology, pharmaceutical research, chemical manufacturing, contract development and manufacturing organizations, computational chemistry, process chemistry, enzyme manufacturing, vendor management, and related areas. The project produced an important business-model pivot. At the beginning of the project, Mutexa was considered primarily as a broad software-as-a-service platform for academic, biotechnology, and pharmaceutical users. Customer discovery showed that this broad model was not the strongest immediate entry point. Instead, the team learned that early adoption is more likely through proof-of-performance projects, pilot programs, direct collaborations, and service-oriented offerings. The strongest early customer segments were enzyme-production contract development and manufacturing organizations (CDMOs), chemical manufacturers, enzyme manufacturers, and process chemistry organizations. The project also clarified Mutexa’s value proposition. Customers were most interested in faster protein optimization, smarter experimental screening libraries, experimentally validated predictions, performance under practical process conditions such as temperature, pH, and solvents, and automation of difficult computational tasks such as sequence screening, stability filtering, solubility filtering, loop-design setup, and enzyme-property prediction. One refined value proposition was that Mutexa could reduce enzyme research and development time by more than 50%, and a related project finding suggested the potential to make screening libraries 10 times smaller.

The intellectual merit of the project lies in connecting advanced computational protein engineering, artificial intelligence, molecular modeling, and enzyme science to real-world design problems. The project showed that the most useful role for AI is not to replace established physics-based modeling tools, but to accelerate, prioritize, and integrate computational workflows so that experimentally testable enzyme candidates can be identified more efficiently. The broader impacts include training students and team members in entrepreneurship, customer discovery, technology translation, industry-facing communication, and commercialization strategy. The project helped trainees understand the difference between technical feasibility and commercial adoption. It also supported the formation of Mutexa Inc. and the development of the MutexaAI website, which introduces MutexaAI as a product from the NSF-supported team.

If successfully commercialized, Mutexa could help make enzyme engineering faster, more efficient, and more accessible. This could support greener chemical synthesis, reduce the need for harsh reagents, improve selectivity in manufacturing, accelerate biotechnology development, and lower barriers for organizations seeking to use biocatalysis and protein engineering.
